title: Hardening Containers: Cap‑Drop, Read‑Only & More 🛡️
description: Use runtime flags and security options to lock down containers and follow the principle of least privilege.

slides.title: Docker Run Security Flags 🛡️
slides.content:
# Your Container Hardening Toolkit

When starting a container, you can add security constraints:

- `--read-only`: mounts the container’s root filesystem as read‑only.
- `--tmpfs /tmp`: provides a writable temporary filesystem for specific directories.
- `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add <CAP>`: drops all capabilities, then adds back only needed ones.
- `--security-opt no-new-privileges`: prevents the container from gaining additional privileges (e.g., via setuid binaries).
- `--security-opt seccomp=<profile>`: applies a custom seccomp profile.
- `--security-opt apparmor=<profile>`: applies AppArmor profile.

Combining these dramatically reduces the attack surface.

slides.title: Example: Hardened Nginx Container 🧱
slides.codeSnippet:
docker run -d \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /var/cache/nginx \
  --tmpfs /var/run \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -p 80:80 \
  nginx:alpine

# Nginx needs /var/cache/nginx and /var/run to be writable, so we mount tmpfs there.

quizData.question: What does the `--read-only` flag do?

options.text: Prevents the container from writing to any file, including volumes
Mounts the container’s root filesystem as read‑only; only mounted volumes and tmpfs are writable
Stops the container from reading files

quizData.explanation: The root filesystem becomes read‑only. Any directories that need writes must be mounted as volumes or tmpfs.

slides.title: `no-new-privileges` – Block Escalation 🚫
slides.content:
# Prevent Setuid Tricks

```bash
docker run --security-opt no-new-privileges …
```

This ensures that even if the container runs a setuid binary, it won’t gain additional capabilities. It’s a kernel feature that prevents privilege escalation.

> Recommended for **every** container that doesn’t need to change UID/GID.

slides.title: Custom Seccomp Profiles 📜
slides.content:
# Restrict Syscalls

Docker’s default seccomp profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls. You can create an even stricter profile.

Example: `deny-all.json` to block all syscalls except a whitelist.

```bash
docker run --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/custom.json …
```

Writing seccomp profiles is advanced, but many tools (like Podman’s `seccomp.json`) provide templates.

> Most containers work fine with the default profile. Custom profiles are for high‑security environments.

quizData.question: The default Docker seccomp profile allows all system calls.
quizData.explanation: The default profile blocks around 44 syscalls (like `reboot`, `kexec_load`) to reduce attack surface.

slides.title: AppArmor & SELinux Profiles 🛡️
slides.content:
# Mandatory Access Control

If your Linux distribution has AppArmor or SELinux enabled, Docker can apply profiles to containers.

- AppArmor:
  ```bash
  docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-nginx …
  ```
- SELinux:
  ```bash
  docker run --security-opt label=type:container_t …
  ```

These policies restrict what files, capabilities, and network a container can access.

> Docker’s default AppArmor profile (`docker-default`) is applied automatically on supported systems.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Combine for Maximum Security
Use `--read-only` + `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` + `--security-opt no-new-privileges` as a baseline for stateless web apps. Only relax as needed.
